description: Formal fallacies, fallacies of relevance, and fallacious appeals, each in four layers, with how to spot and answer them.

depth.picture: Arguments that fail because of their shape, whatever they are about.
depth.mechanism: A formal fallacy has a structure that does not guarantee its conclusion. You can show it invalid by keeping the same form and swapping in content where the premises are plainly true and the conclusion plainly false.
depth.detail: The common ones involve conditionals and categories: affirming the consequent, denying the antecedent, and the undistributed middle. The counterexample method is the standard test: if the same form gives a true conclusion in one case and a false one in another, the form cannot be trusted. Probability has its own formal slips, such as the conjunction fallacy.
depth.principles: Because the flaw is in the form, it can be found without knowing anything about the topic. That is what makes formal logic useful: it checks reasoning as a pattern, before you have to argue about the facts.

depth.picture: If it rained, the street is wet. The street is wet. So it rained. The last step doesn't follow.
depth.mechanism: A conditional says that the first thing leads to the second, not the reverse. Finding the second thing tells you nothing certain about the first, because other causes could have produced it.
depth.detail: Form: if P then Q; Q; therefore P. Counterexample: if it is a dog, it is an animal; it is an animal; so it is a dog. In science the mistake appears as taking a successful prediction as proof of the theory: the theory predicted the result, the result happened, but other theories might have predicted it too. What it does give is some support, in the probabilistic sense, not a guarantee.
depth.principles: A conditional gives a sufficient condition, not a necessary one: P being true is enough for Q, but Q can be true for many other reasons. Confusing the direction of an if-then is among the most common logical errors, and it is why confirmation is weaker than refutation.

depth.picture: If it rained, the street is wet. It didn't rain. So the street is dry. But something else might have wet it.
depth.mechanism: The rule says rain is enough to make the street wet. It does not say rain is the only way. So the absence of rain leaves the question open.
depth.detail: Form: if P then Q; not P; therefore not Q. Counterexample: if you are in Paris you are in France; you are not in Paris; so you are not in France. The valid neighbor is modus tollens, which denies the consequent instead. People often make the error when a rule sounds like a two-way street, such as promotions: if you work hard you will be promoted; you did not work hard; so you will not be promoted.
depth.principles: Sufficient conditions are not necessary conditions. To reason validly from what is missing you need the reverse claim: if and only if. Otherwise other routes to the same result are left unaccounted for.

depth.picture: All dogs are mammals. All cats are mammals. So all dogs are cats. Sharing a category doesn't make two things the same.
depth.mechanism: In a syllogism, the middle term must cover the whole of at least one category. When it only overlaps part of each, the two ends are linked to it but not to each other.
depth.detail: Form: all A are B; all C are B; therefore all A are C. Venn diagram: draw circles for A, C, and B with A and C both inside B but not overlapping; the conclusion is not shown. Real-world versions: all fascists hate communists; she hates communists; so she is a fascist. The hidden move is treating a shared property as if it defined the group.
depth.principles: Shared membership shows only that two things overlap somewhere, not that one fits inside the other. Valid categorical reasoning needs containment relationships that chain together, which is what distribution of the middle term captures.

depth.picture: Thinking that two things together are more likely than one of them alone.
depth.mechanism: A vivid, detailed story feels more plausible, so we rate it above a plainer statement. But adding detail can only make something less likely, since each detail must also be true.
depth.detail: Kahneman and Tversky's Linda problem: Linda is outspoken, bright, and concerned about social justice. Which is more probable, that she is a bank teller, or a bank teller active in the feminist movement? Most people choose the second, but it is a subset of the first, so it cannot be more probable. Rule: P(A and B) is never greater than P(A). It is a case of judging by representativeness instead of probability.
depth.principles: Probability obeys strict rules that intuition does not, and story-like coherence is a poor guide to likelihood. Detail adds persuasiveness while subtracting probability, which is why forecasters and lawyers alike can mislead with rich scenarios.

depth.picture: Deciding a claim is false because someone argued for it badly.
depth.mechanism: You spot a flaw in the case for a claim and jump to rejecting the claim. But the claim might be true anyway, supported by a better argument you have not heard.
depth.detail: Form: argument X for claim C is fallacious; therefore C is false. Example: you say we should recycle because everyone does (a bandwagon appeal); I point out the fallacy; you conclude recycling is pointless. A fair response is that the reason offered fails, but the claim may still stand. The remedy is to ask for a better argument or to look for one yourself.
depth.principles: The truth of a claim and the quality of an argument for it are separate. Poor reasons prove nothing either way. Recognizing this stops fallacy-spotting from becoming a way of dismissing conclusions one dislikes.

depth.picture: Fallacies that change the subject: they answer a different, easier question than the one that was asked.
depth.mechanism: Instead of engaging the actual claim, the arguer attacks the person, distorts the position, raises a distraction, or points elsewhere. The argument feels like a rebuttal but leaves the original claim untouched.
depth.detail: Members include ad hominem, straw man, red herring, tu quoque, whataboutism, and the genetic fallacy. To spot one, restate the original question and ask whether the reply actually bears on it. To answer one, name what was skipped and return to it politely: that may be true of me, but does it change whether the claim is right?
depth.principles: Relevance is the minimum requirement for a reason: it must bear on the truth of the conclusion. These fallacies work because people, especially in heated exchanges, respond to social cues more readily than to logic.

depth.picture: Answering the person instead of the argument.
depth.mechanism: You point to a flaw in the speaker (their motives, character, or background) and treat it as if it refuted what they said. The claim itself has not been addressed.
depth.detail: Abusive form: you can't trust her, she has been wrong before. Circumstantial form: he would say that, he works for the company. It is not a fallacy to note a real conflict of interest as a reason to look harder at a claim; it becomes one when the flaw is treated as proof that the claim is false. Test: would the argument be any less valid if someone else had made it?
depth.principles: Truth is independent of the speaker. A bad person can say true things and a good person false ones, so the argument must be judged on its merits. Character can matter to how much to trust testimony, but never to whether a valid argument is valid.

depth.picture: Misrepresenting someone's view as weaker or sillier than it is, then knocking that version down.
depth.mechanism: You restate their position in an exaggerated or distorted form, defeat the distortion, and act as though you have defeated their actual position. The original argument is left standing.
depth.detail: Common techniques: oversimplifying, taking a quote out of context, attacking an extreme example, or attributing a whole worldview based on one remark. Example: A: we should spend a little more on cycle lanes. B: so you want to ban cars? Defense: restate their view and ask, is this what you mean? The constructive counterpart is steelmanning.
depth.principles: A straw man wins only by changing the topic. It persuades an audience that has not heard the real position, and it corrodes debate by teaching people that their views will be caricatured. Fair restatement is the price of a real disagreement.

depth.picture: Bringing up something irrelevant to lead the discussion away from the point.
depth.mechanism: A new, interesting or emotionally charged topic is introduced. The conversation follows it, and the original question is quietly forgotten or never answered.
depth.detail: The name is said to come from dragging a smelly fish across a trail to throw hounds off the scent. Examples: asked about a budget shortfall, a politician talks about the opponent's record; asked whether a claim is true, someone starts on how it is used. Response: acknowledge the new point briefly, then return to the original question. The distractions are often true, just beside the point.
depth.principles: Attention is limited, and a discussion can only follow one line at a time. A red herring exploits that, so keeping track of the original question is a discipline that protects the argument from being hijacked, by others or by your own wandering.

depth.picture: Answering criticism with you do it too.
depth.mechanism: Instead of addressing whether the claim is right, you point out that the critic does not follow their own advice. The implied message is that they have no standing to say it.
depth.detail: Latin for you also. Example: a doctor tells a patient to stop smoking, and the patient replies that the doctor smokes. The doctor's hypocrisy affects how credible they are as a role model, but not whether smoking is harmful. It is legitimate to note inconsistency when it bears on sincerity or on a claim about the critic's own behavior; it is a fallacy when used to dismiss the point.
depth.principles: A claim stands or falls on the evidence, not on the consistency of the person making it. Hypocrisy is a moral fault of the speaker; it is not a refutation of what they said.

depth.picture: Answering an accusation by raising a different wrong: but what about when they did it?
depth.mechanism: You deflect from the issue on the table by pointing to a similar or unrelated failing on the other side. The conversation shifts from whether this happened to who else has done something.
depth.detail: A form of tu quoque and red herring, made prominent in Cold War propaganda. It is not always fallacious: comparison can reveal a double standard, and consistency is a fair thing to ask for. The fallacy is using another wrong as if it cancelled this one. Test: if the other example were entirely fixed tomorrow, would the original claim still be true?
depth.principles: Two wrongs do not cancel: an accusation can be true even if others are guilty too. Insisting on dealing with one issue at a time keeps discussion from becoming an endless scoreboard where nothing is ever resolved.

depth.picture: Judging an idea by where it came from rather than by whether it is any good.
depth.mechanism: You dismiss or accept a claim because of its origin: who first said it, when, or under what circumstances. The claim's merits are never examined.
depth.detail: Example: that theory was first proposed by a discredited person, so it must be wrong. Or, this custom is ancient, so it must be wise. Origins can be relevant to how much scrutiny a claim deserves and to how reliable a source is. The fallacy is to treat them as decisive. Many good ideas came from odd places, such as the benzene ring famously imagined in a dream.
depth.principles: The truth of an idea is separate from its history. Origins explain how we came to hold a belief, not whether it is justified. Evaluating on merits protects against both undeserved suspicion and undeserved reverence.

depth.picture: Arguments that lean on something that feels like a reason but is not one: authority, emotion, nature, tradition, novelty, popularity, or ignorance.
depth.mechanism: Each appeal points to a feature that is often correlated with truth, so it carries weight, but is treated as decisive. The fallacy lies in the leap from a clue to a conclusion.
depth.detail: The main ones: appeal to authority, to emotion, to nature, to tradition, to novelty, to the crowd (bandwagon), to ignorance, and to consequences. Each can be legitimate in moderation: expert opinion is evidence, popular belief is evidence, and a tested tradition may hold hard-won wisdom. The test is whether the appeal is offered as one piece of evidence or as the whole argument.
depth.principles: These appeals are shortcuts that mostly work, which is why they are persuasive. They fail when we stop asking why the authority, feeling, or crowd should be right in this case.

depth.picture: An expert says so, therefore it's true.
depth.mechanism: You accept a claim solely because someone with status endorses it, and treat the endorsement as the reason to believe. The evidence the expert relies on is never examined.
depth.detail: Deferring to expertise is often sensible, since nobody can check everything. It becomes a fallacy when the person is not an expert in the relevant field, when experts disagree, when the authority is only a celebrity, when the claim is outside consensus, or when authority is the only support offered. Better questions: are they qualified on this topic? do other qualified people agree? what is their evidence?
depth.principles: Expertise raises the probability that a claim is right, but does not make it so. Authority is a proxy for evidence, valuable when we cannot examine the evidence directly and reliable to the degree the field itself is reliable.

depth.picture: Using fear, pity, anger, or hope in place of a reason.
depth.mechanism: You stir a strong feeling and let it stand in for evidence. The audience feels the claim is important or true, and stops asking whether it is.
depth.detail: Examples: showing a sad image to prove a policy works, or scaring people about consequences without evidence they will occur. Emotion is not illegitimate in an argument: if a situation is truly frightening, fear is a fitting response, and emotions can motivate action. It is a fallacy when the feeling replaces the case rather than accompanying it. Test: if the emotion were removed, would any reason remain?
depth.principles: Feelings are part of how humans decide, but they are responses to what we believe, not evidence for it. An appeal to emotion is honest when the emotion is proportionate to the facts, and manipulative when it goes around them.

depth.picture: It's natural, so it's good; it's unnatural, so it's bad.
depth.mechanism: You treat natural as meaning safe, healthy, or right, and artificial as meaning harmful. The word natural does the persuading, and no evidence about the actual thing is required.
depth.detail: Counterexamples are easy: arsenic, hemlock, malaria, and earthquakes are natural; eyeglasses, vaccines, and antibiotics are not. The word natural is also vague: does it mean not made by humans, common in the wild, or as originally found? Marketing uses it constantly. Related is the naturalistic fallacy, deriving what ought to be from what is.
depth.principles: Nature has no interest in human welfare. Whether something is good or safe is a fact about its effects and can only be settled by evidence about those effects, not by its origin or by how it is labeled.

depth.picture: We have always done it this way, so it must be right.
depth.mechanism: You treat a practice's age as a reason to keep it. The fact that it lasted stands in for any case that it works or is right.
depth.detail: Traditions can carry accumulated wisdom, tested by generations, and the burden on those who would change them can reasonably be real. But many longstanding practices, from bloodletting to legal inequality, were mistaken or unjust. Chesterton's fence offers a balanced view: do not remove something until you understand why it was put there, and then judge it on its merits.
depth.principles: Survival is weak evidence of merit, because practices persist for reasons that have nothing to do with being good: habit, power, inertia, or fear of change. Age is a clue to look for reasons, not itself a reason.

depth.picture: It's new, so it's better.
depth.mechanism: You treat the newness of an idea or product as a reason to prefer it. The comparison with what came before is skipped.
depth.detail: Marketing thrives on it: new and improved. Newer things are sometimes better, since technology and knowledge advance, but sometimes worse, unproven, or just different. The mirror image of the appeal to tradition, they are both ways of using a date instead of evidence. To check, compare the actual performance of the new and the old on the things that matter.
depth.principles: Time of origin says nothing about quality. Both novelty and antiquity are surface features, and honest evaluation looks past them to how well the thing does its job.

depth.picture: Everyone believes it, so it must be true.
depth.mechanism: You treat widespread belief or popularity as a reason for accepting a claim, without examining why so many hold it.
depth.detail: Also called argumentum ad populum. It is a matter of degree: when many independent people, each with good access to the facts, agree, that is real evidence (the wisdom of crowds). But belief spreads by imitation and social pressure too, and majorities have often been wrong: the Earth is flat, the four humors. Ask whether the believers arrived at it independently and whether they had reason to know.
depth.principles: People conform for many reasons besides truth, so the number of believers measures social influence at least as much as evidence. Popularity is a clue about what people think, and only a weak clue about what is so.

depth.picture: No one has proven it false, so it must be true. Or the reverse.
depth.mechanism: You take the absence of disproof as support for a claim, which quietly shifts the burden of proof onto the skeptic.
depth.detail: Form: there is no evidence against P, therefore P; or no evidence for P, therefore not-P. Sometimes absence of evidence is evidence of absence: if a large animal lived in a small park, we would expect to see it. But for claims that are by nature hard to test, lack of disproof shows nothing. Bertrand Russell's celestial teapot makes the point: no one can disprove it, and no one should therefore believe it.
depth.principles: The person making a claim must support it. Ignorance is not knowledge, and uncertainty is not a point for either side; it just means the question is open.

depth.picture: It can't be true because it would be terrible. Or it must be true because it would be wonderful.
depth.mechanism: You judge whether a claim is true by whether its consequences are pleasant or harmful. What you want to be so takes the place of what the evidence shows.
depth.detail: Examples: that diagnosis can't be right, I couldn't bear it; or, of course the plan will work, otherwise we are ruined. The consequences of a claim can rightly matter for what to do about it or how carefully to check it, but they have no bearing on whether it is true. Wishful thinking is the everyday form; it is also related to motivated reasoning.
depth.principles: Reality does not adjust to our preferences. Facts are established by evidence, and desirability enters only afterward, when deciding what to do given the facts. Keeping the two apart is a basic discipline of honest thinking.
